title: Does the presence of others help or hurt performance?

readings.title: Source 1: Source 1: Typing in front of an audience
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether being watched changes performance differently on an easy and a hard task.

Participants

96 university students (ages 18 to 24) in Ontario, Canada, all experienced typists, volunteered and gave informed consent.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to type alone or with two observers watching from behind. Each student typed two passages: an easy one in English and a hard one with English words written backward. The researchers counted correct words per minute.

Results

On the easy passage, students who were watched typed 58 correct words per minute, compared with 52 alone. On the hard passage, students who were watched typed 14 correct words per minute, compared with 19 alone.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 2: Source 2: Shouting alone or in a group
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether people put in less effort when their effort is combined with others' and cannot be measured separately.

Participants

60 high school students (ages 15 to 17) in Florida took part with a parent's consent and their own assent.

Method

Wearing headphones that played noise, each student was asked to shout as loudly as possible. Students did this alone, and also in groups of 6 where they were told only the group's total volume would be recorded. In fact, a separate microphone measured each student's own volume in both conditions. Afterward, students were told about the hidden microphones and why they were needed.

Results

Students shouted at a mean of 88 decibels alone and 81 decibels in the groups of 6. Ten of the students, in a separate session, were told their own volume would be posted on a screen even in the group; their mean volume in the group was 87 decibels.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 3: Source 3: Runners with and without a pacer
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether experienced runners run faster when another runner is beside them.

Participants

40 members of running clubs in Colorado (ages 25 to 45; 22 women and 18 men), each with at least 3 years of training, gave informed consent.

Method

Each runner ran 1 mile on a track twice, a week apart, in a random order: once alone and once with another club member running alongside at the same pace. A stopwatch recorded each time.

Results

The mean time was 7 minutes 12 seconds when running alone and 6 minutes 58 seconds when running with another runner, 14 seconds faster. 31 of the 40 runners were faster with a partner.

Invented study for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based on at least one of the provided sources that responds to the question: Does the presence of others help or hurt performance?

rubric.point: States a defensible claim that answers whether others' presence helps or hurts performance
accept: Others help performance on easy or well-practiced tasks but hurt it on hard tasks and when effort is pooled
The presence of others helps performance when a person's own work is visible
The presence of others can hurt performance

parts.sample: The presence of other people helps performance on easy or well-practiced tasks when each person's work is visible, but hurts it on hard tasks and when individual effort cannot be identified.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from one source and cites it
accept: In Source 1, watched students typed more correct words per minute on the easy passage (58 versus 52) but fewer on the hard passage (14 versus 19)
In Source 3, experienced runners ran 14 seconds faster with a partner

parts.sample: According to Source 1, students who were watched typed 58 correct words per minute on an easy passage, compared with 52 alone, but only 14 on a hard passage, compared with 19 alone.

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim
accept: Being watched improved the easy task and worsened the hard one, which matches the claim

rubric.point: Applies a psychology concept (not a restricted term) to the evidence and links it to the claim

parts.sample: This supports my claim through social facilitation: the presence of others raises arousal, which strengthens a person's most practiced response. For experienced typists, typing ordinary English is practiced, so being watched made them faster; typing backward words is new, so the strengthened response (typing words forward) caused more errors. The same audience helped one task and hurt the other, as my claim says.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from a different source and cites it
accept: Source 2 found students shouted at 81 decibels in groups where only the total was recorded, versus 88 alone, and 87 when their own volume was posted

parts.sample: Source 2 found that students shouted at a mean of 88 decibels alone but only 81 decibels in a group where only the total volume was recorded. When their own volume was posted even in the group, they shouted at 87 decibels.

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim
accept: Students put in less effort when their effort was hidden in the group total, and effort returned when it was visible

rubric.point: Applies a different concept from B(ii) (not a restricted term) and links it to the claim

parts.sample: This supports the second part of my claim through social loafing: people put in less effort when their individual contribution is pooled and cannot be identified. Students shouted less loudly when only the group total counted, so the presence of others hurt performance. When each student's volume was posted, the loafing nearly disappeared (87 decibels), which shows that it is hidden effort, not other people as such, that lowers performance.
